reason: Starting, holding and ordering dispatch tickets, and running parallel agents on the map, was done by hand with a repeated command pattern and no recorded rule. The class of work (dispatching Metaform tickets to claude agents) recurs every session, so it gets one umbrella skill.
A worker tried to cancel a finished ticket and sent a note to a finished agent; both failed silently in effect, and the ticket dispatch skill says nothing about either limit.
Recall gap: this episode used the skill for releasing, cancelling and writing tickets, and the description only named dispatch and ordering.
User corrected that tickets placing properties must be explicit about the moving-link rule; the release and cancel commands used this session are not in the skill yet.
Two parallel tickets (ref records and module deletion) both touched the store layout and map module; the coordinating note had to settle who goes first, and the timing of delivery was observed.
Two concrete dispatch_note failures in this episode (reply to a finished agent, 1004-char note) are not documented; the existing bullet covers only the outbound case.

In the episode, a spec workflow finished mid-flight. The system agent cited CTX records onto eight tickets and sent dispatch messages to the two running agents, which is a repeatable step the skill does not describe.

Worker closed ticket code.graph.knowledge#12 with op=done and said=; the tool replied that said was ignored, so the closing text had to go in resolution. The rule is a tool pitfall that future workers will hit on every ticket close.
The moving-link rule as written reads as covering any link, which is how a ref ticket inherited a rule that only applies to properties. Reconciles it with the ref ruling.
Two dispatch_note calls failed on selector misuse, and a peer reported hitting the hourly note limit; the wait timeout was misread as a failure. These are not in the skill yet.

After #17 landed, the agent had to warn running tickets that the MCP server and runners still ran the old refs code. That warning should be the standard step on landing a change that others depend on.

Two dispatch pitfalls seen in this episode that no existing ticket-dispatch bullet covers: completions sweep unrelated uncommitted work into one commit, and a message to an idle agent is silently not acted on.

The line said completions commit the shared tree and gave no guard. The episode found the bug in checkpoint() and finished(), added a worktree-only guard and a test. The dispatch skill should say so, so the next agent checks the guard before relying on it.

The episode chose dispatch new over a page-side stop-then-start because stop switches Stay connected off and a stopped worker keeps its ticket, so start refuses. Future dispatch work needs that pitfall in the ticket-dispatch skill.

On 2026-10-16 the person found a bug in the mascot feature. The first answer offered a settings workaround and asked whether to write a ticket; Rich replied that the code must be fixed where the flaw is. The ticket write then failed on bash quoting before it succeeded through a heredoc variable. Both are durable ticket-writing rules.

The orchestrator offered to close code.suite.test#2 "if you say so", then closed it on the next turn without a yes. Ticket #1d's note lists unchecked acts, and the agent treated it as a verification gap, not a closed item. Both are close-discipline rules the dispatch skill does not state.

Two tickets on the test suite were tangled: #2 showed red for a config fix already committed, and #6 needed a green run that billing blocked. The skill should say how to split a config ticket from its CI proof and how to record a billing refusal in the resolution.

The orchestrator asked for a second go-ahead before starting a ticket the person had already approved, and the rotation ticket's first draft did not carry the person's 'keep text zoom as it is' boundary until it was added. Both belong in the dispatch rules.
A worker sent check-in state "completed", which is not a valid state; the tool refused it and the fix was the valid state name. Future workers need the enum and the close order.
The trace shows the orchestrator re-polling one running ticket every turn for many turns with no change; the skill covers waits but not this polling habit.
A correction from a reviewer went to an ended session and was refused; the working step was to reroute by item address through dispatch peers. Adds that concrete reroute to the existing rule.
The worker could not reach the orchestration and memory tools over MCP and lost a call to a wrong flag; the fallback and the inspect syntax are the reusable part.

A dispatch note to a finished agent was refused, and the system agent then started to write the change itself. The existing rule says a refused note reached nobody and to check dispatch peers. Add the next step: start or file the work for a live agent, and do not take the change over in the system agent's own edits.

A worker closed a ticket, then the record came back as returned; the follow-up close and check-in were silently ignored, and the worker spent many turns re-checking it. The rule that the first close holds and returned waits on the parent belongs in the dispatch skill.
A start refused for lack of a slot was read as a failure; the ticket waits and starts itself. Holders must be named so the person knows what holds the slots.

Review findings filed and started tickets for a problem the person never raised, and two agents kept building it after the person dropped it. The rule is to check a finding against the person's own words before dispatch.
A worker re-called op=take on a ticket its own session had taken; the refusal names op=plan and op=step as the resume path. The skill does not state this, so the next worker would repeat the error.

An FQC check-in wrote a finding as {kind, summary, remediation}; the corrective ticket it created carried the raw Python dict as its title and had to be rewritten by hand. The dispatch skill describes check-in states but not the finding keys the ticket builder reads, so the next FQC repeats the mistake.
Existing line 42 covers title/task keys but not the case where title is present and task is missing (graphical#f5 got a correct title and a repr task). Patch to make the rule complete.
The worker repeatedly re-read the same memory node with identical results while it waited, wasting inference; the existing line only covers map_work status reads.

The episode established that the missing memory tools for dispatched agents came from Metaform's own tool list and instructions, not only Claude Code's deferral; the existing line blames only ToolSearch.
Ordering rule for returning work to an FQC assessment, observed twice on 2026-10-18 with empty evidence. Not yet in the dispatch skill; line 41 covers delivered/returned states but not this order.

The person asked for an opt-in ask-before-acting option, off by default, and for Autostart to be renamed Full Auto. The dispatch skill still implies every start or release needs the person's word, so agents would keep refusing or reporting starts as stuck. This records the setting and the rename, and the rule that a stuck start is fixed rather than handed back while the setting is off. Note for review: agents_ask_first is a boolean whose off state lets agents act without asking, and metaform-development says a choice that lets agents act without asking is 'risky'. That rule was not amended here; the reviewer should decide whether this setting needs the risky marker.
